Introduction

Horsetooth Reservoir, located west of Fort Collins, Colorado, is a vital part of the region’s water supply and recreational landscape. Constructed in 1949 as part of the Colorado-Big Thompson Project, the reservoir plays a key role in storing water diverted from the western slope of the Rocky Mountains through a system of tunnels and canals (Colorado-Big Thompson Project). With a surface area of approximately 1,900 acres and a capacity of 156,735 acre-feet, Horsetooth Reservoir provides water for agricultural irrigation, municipal needs, and hydropower generation (Colorado-Big Thompson Project; Horsetooth Reservoir). Over the years, it has become a popular destination for outdoor enthusiasts, offering activities such as boating, fishing, hiking, and camping. Beyond its recreational use, the reservoir is also an important environmental and water management asset for Northern Colorado, ensuring a steady water supply in a region prone to droughts and growing urban demands (Colorado-Big Thompson Project).

Methods

For this experiment, an entire profile of the reservoir was taken, along with Secchi depth, algae and zooplankton samples, and multiple water samples to process (NH4/NO3), (TP), and (TDN/TDC). A pontoon boat allowed access to a section of the reservoir with maximum depth to complete the reservoir profile (fig. X). This allowed for a clear measure of stratification between the epilimnion and hypolimnion. Using a handheld Sonde sensor, measurements of temperature, pH, conductivity, salinity, dissolved oxygen, and chlorophyll-a were collected in meter increments for 20 meters. This data was displayed on the Sonde screen and documented in a journal. Next Secchi depth was calculated with Secchi disk from the mean for maximum viewable depth descending and ascending. This was collected three times and averaged. Algae and Zooplankton samples were collected using a Zooplankton net with a basket. The net was dipped into the epilimnion and quickly raised to catch the samples. This was done 4-5 times per sample to ensure a large sample size. The nets were sprayed with distilled water in a squeeze bottle to concentrate the sample into the basket. The samples were rinsed into a 50ml falcon tube and filled to 40ml. 0.5ml of Lugol’s was added to preserve the solution. These samples were immediately entered into an ice-cold cooler. Using a Van Dorn sampler with line and messenger, hypolimnion and epilimnion samples were collected. Using an opaque liter bottle, a sample was collected 1 meter below the surface and 1 meter below the thermocline at (X) meters below the surface found from the profile. Between each sample, the bottle was rinsed with the correct sample collected to prevent the mixing of samples. For each sample of (NH4/NO3), (TP), and (TDN/TDC), an extra was collected securely, each was collected into four unique tubes, two for epilimnium and two for hypolimnium. For (TP) and (NH4/NO3), samples were collected in 15ml falcon tubes filled to the 10ml mark. Before filling the tubes, the samples passed through a GFF filter in a syringe. To prepare these, the GFF filter was placed into the chamber using forceps and then attached to the syringe. The volume passed through the GFF was documented and the GFF was quickly folded and secured into aluminum foil with forceps, double-folded, and added to the cooler. This was used to calculate chlorophyll a. The (TDN/TDC) samples were collected in 50ml tubes filled to the 40ml mark. Each tube and GGF was labeled with name, date, group #, sample location in water collum, depth, volume of water, and parameter.

Results (Interpretation)

Figure 1 shows the depth profile for Horsetooth Reservoir dissolved oxygen in early September. The figure shows a sinuous pattern, with the shallower depths having more DO and the deeper depths having less DO.

Figure 2 shows the temperature profile of Horsetooth Reservoir. The figure shows a similar sinuous pattern as Figure 1. The figure shows shallower depths having warmer temperatures whilst the deeper depths have cooler temperatures.

Figures 1 and 2 both show roughly the same respective values from 0 to 10 meters. This is to be expected due to the mixed layer of the epilimnion being consistent throughout.

Figure 3 shows the depth profile for Horsetooth Reservoir pH. This pattern is still sinuous, however unlike the pattern in Figures 1 and 2. The reservoir has a relatively neutral pH, with values ranging from 7.0 to 7.8. The upper layers start around 7.4, then the pH increases with depth to about 7.6 until about 10 m where the pH goes back down to about 7.2 around 15 m. The hypolimnion shows a wide range in pH with values at both 7.0 and 7.8. The pH of the reservoir can tell us a multitude of things such as the buffering capacity, microbial activity, and water quality.

Figure 4 shows the standard curve for the total nitrogen concentration. There is a linear relationship between the TN concentration and area, with a slope of ~1. This value along with the values of the standard curve are rounded with ggpmisc for consistency. This curve shows that the thermocline and stratification of the lake has no influence on the total nitrogen between the hypolimnion and epilimnion. This shows a lacking correlation between nutrients and stratification and suggests consistent nutrient inputs.

Figure 5 shows the total nitrogen values in both the epilimnion and hypolimnion taken by every group excluding group 9. These values range from 0 to 12.5 mg/L. Most of these values range from 4 to 8 mg/L in both layers of the reservoir. The total nitrogen of a lake is a key indicator of the lake’s nutrient status, ecological health, and trophic state. The high nitrogen in Horsetooth suggests nutrient pollution.

Figure 6 shows the chlorophyll A values in the epilimnion taken by every group and the average of those values. These values range from 0.001 to 0.514 ug/L, with the average at 0.222. These values are fairly varied with no distinct pattern. This is likely due to incorrect sampling and/or data analyzation. Chlorophyll A values are a good indicator of the lake’s biological productivity and ecological health. The values collected here show minimal algal growth.

Figure 7 shows the comparison of dissolved organic carbon in the epilimnion and hypolimnion, values taken from all groups. There does not seem to be a consistent pattern across all groups, but many of the values fall from 1 to 2.5 mg/L. This once again could be due to incorrect sampling and/or data analyzation. The DOC provides insights into the lake’s chemical composition, ecological processes, and interactions with its surrounding environment. The values collected here seem to be low to moderate, telling us that the reservoir has low to moderate organic matter inputs.

Figure 8 shows the secchi depths taken by each group. The figure shows that some groups took multiple depths while a couple only took one depth. All depths range from 2.125 to 3 m in depth, with an average of 2.6 m. All groups but one got at least one secchi depth at 2.5 m. The secchi depth measures water clarity which tells us information about the lake’s physical, biological, and chemical characteristics. The secchi depth value we collected seems to be moderate.

Discussion

  1. There was a difference in DOC between depths, although it does not seem to be much of a difference. This difference can be attributed to the increased primary productivity from phytoplankton and algae in the epilimnion. The hypolimnion often gets less terrestrial and atmospheric inputs of organic matter. Another thing that might affect this difference is runoff containing organic matter, such as fertilizer from agriculture.

  2. There was a difference in total nitrogen between depths, with the epilimnion generally having higher values than the hypolimnion, though the difference was relatively small. This is likely due to summer stratification, which limits nutrient exchange between layers. In the epilimnion, biological activity such as nitrogen uptake by phytoplankton and surface inputs may contribute to higher nitrogen levels. In contrast, the hypolimnion may experience limited oxygen availability, which can inhibit nitrification and promote processes like ammonium accumulation or denitrification, reducing total nitrogen.

  3. Our Horsetooth Reservoir data can be compared to many other different reservoirs within the state as well as out of state. For this comparison, we chose to compare it to Dillon reservoir, due to its similarity in total volume, surface area, and distance to Horsetooth Reservoir. According to a report by the EPA on the water quality parameters of the reservoir, a survey was done for vertically integrated samples of DO, Temperature, pH, Total Nitrogen, Chlorophyll A, and Secchi Depth. Due to the type of data collected, we will compare the median values taken within this assessment to our charts provided in this report. The first parameter comparison is Dissolved Oxygen by milligrams per liter, with Dillon Reservoir integrated samples at a median of 7.0 mg/L (Environmental Protection Agency). Comparing this to our depth profile for DO at Horsetooth, we find that our epilimnion was around 7.0 with the metalimnion around 4.0 and the hypolimnion have DO at 0 mg/L at a depth of 25 meters. Seeing this, we can see that the median would be much lower than Dillon Reservoir, illustrated much lower dissolved oxygen values by ~3 mg/L. This difference, although speculative, could be attributed to water temperature, mixing dynamics of both lakes, as well as reservoir inputs from high alpine rivers such as the Blue, Snake and Tenmile which would likely be more oxygenated than the water from the Colorado Big Thompson Project that inflows via canal.
    The temperature median of Dillon Reservoir is 12.4 degrees Celsius. Our profile of Horsetooth Reservoir illustrated a depth profile tracking like DO, with temperatures at the surface of ~21C and lows of ~13C. Similar to DO, we can see that Dillon reservoir has lower temperatures than Horsetooth, once more likely due to inflow sources, as well as elevation differential, with Horsetooth at 3430 ft and Dillon at 9016 ft. The Dillon Reservoir pH median was reported by the EPA as 7.6, which compares to our measurement of roughly 7.3 standard units, which illustrates very similar pH levels for both reservoirs. Although our measurements were not integrated as the median was for EPA-Dillon Reservoir, our profile illustrates a strong consistent pH variation with many of the values between 7.2 and 7.6, therefore Dillon reservoir has a slightly higher pH level.
    The Total Nitrogen (mg/L) of Dillon Reservoir was reported by the EPA Eutrophication Study as 0.225mg/L. This is a drastic comparison to our Horsetooth Samples, across groups in our Figure 5, we find that our epilimnion and hypolimnion values have little to no strong difference, but the values consistently range between 4 and 8 mg/L Total Nitrogen. This difference strongly suggests external inputs of nitrogen loading to Horsetooth Reservoir, likely due to urban non-point source inputs, fertilizer runoff and nitrogen deposition to the surface of the lake. These values deserve further investigation to determine any spatial or temporal variability affecting TN values in Horsetooth Reservoir. By implementing more TN samples from across the lake as well as through time, we could better understand the increase in nitrogen levels found in the reservoir, risking eutrophication and algal blooms in Horsetooth.
    Chlorophyll A values were also surveyed by the EPA in their report, finding a median of 2.3 ug/L. In comparison, our profile of Horsetooth Reservoir in Figure 6 ranges from 0.001 to 0.514 ug/L, with the average at 0.222. Our profile demonstrates likely problems in the sampling method, as there is no distinct Chlorophyll A pattern across groups. With such low values, we should have seen higher Chlorophyll A values. Because Secchi depth and Chl A values are highly linked due to attenuation of insolation being caused by phytoplankton in the lake water column, we can infer that our data would support each other only if Chl A was lower in Horsetooth and Secchi depth was higher.
    Comparing Secchi depth between reservoirs, we find the EPA Dillon Reservoir median at 5.8 m and Horsetooth Reservoir Secchi depth mean at 2.6m. Although there are many factors that influence these values, and it is not a direct comparison between median and mean values, we find that there is a strong indication that one of these parameters is not accurate. As Secchi depth procedure is much simpler than Chl A sampling and measurement, we can conclude with reasonable doubt that our Chlorophyll A values are not accurate and likely need to be discarded due to sampling error.
    This EPA report for Dillon Reservoir was utilized and cited for comparison due to its completeness in the parameters measured, reliability of the organization providing the data, as well as the inclusion of methods in the report, furthering the usefulness and reliability of the dataset. Consideration for this data must include that there are significant temporal differences in the dataset for Dillon Reservoir versus Horsetooth as the EPA report is fairly old, as well as the lack of Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC) for Dillon Reservoir. Although these considerations are necessary, this dataset is useful for comparison between reservoirs and was found to be the most complete and easily available comparison reservoir data.

  4. Explaining the similarities between these two reservoirs, we can see that stratification occurs in both lakes, due to the seasonal temperature patterns seen in Colorado, both in the lower elevation plains around Horsetooth as well as in the Rocky Mountains surrounding Dillon Reservoir. Additionally, we found that they both held similar pH levels, which indicates that both reservoirs are similar in their trophic state, pollution levels, as well as geological and soil composition. Limnologically, both lakes certainly demonstrate mixing regimes in the epilimnion as well as dimictic patterns, which result in similar yet small differences in standard parameters such as pH and DO that are strongly associated with the mixing pattern of the reservoir.
    Explaining the differences between these two reservoirs is certainly more challenging, as there are many factors that make these reservoirs different, certainly influencing their water quality parameters. Limnologically, the reservoirs sit at very different elevations, resulting in definite climate differences, resulting in their different temperature regimes as Dillon Reservoir sits double the elevation, experiencing much larger cooling forces than Fort Collins. Additionally, nutrient inputs to Horsetooth Reservoir by nearby agricultural and urban runoff certainly contribute to higher Total Nitrogen levels in Horsetooth Reservoir. In comparison, a smaller urban drainage area and very low agricultural drainage area certainly limits the nitrogen loading we find in the EPA report.

  5. Our study conducted at Horsetooth Reservoir may face several limitations and potential errors that could impact the insights gained from the data. The samples were collected at ~12:00 PM, which may not represent the full daily variability of parameters like oxygen, pH, and nutrients that change throughout the day due to biological activity. Another error could come from sampling in only one area of the reservoir. Sampling from only one site in the reservoir limits the ability to understand how environmental conditions might differ across the entire water body. Variations in wind speed and temperature (especially during seasonal transitions) can affect surface water conditions (e.g., mixing, evaporation rates) and could skew our results. Ways to address these issues include taking multiple samples at different times of day to better understand parameters that change throughout the day such as oxygen and nutrients. This could also include sampling at multiple sites on the reservoir to get a better understanding of the whole reservoir, not just one area. Lastly, sampling across multiple days would help us understand variations that occur due to wind speed and temperature.

Conclusion

Horsetooth Reservoir is a vastly impactful reservoir because of its importance to the northern Colorado front range as a source of drinking and running water, as well as a vast habitat and resource for wildlife in the region. That said, our collection of data and references of the reservoir has indicated it had entered a eutrophic state. With a mean secchi depth of ~2.6 m and a mean nitrogen range from 4 to 8 mg/L, reference data indicated that these levels far exceed the mean oligotrophic values and indicate a eutrophic state (Poikane & Kelly G 2022). This access of nutrients has led to a bloom in green algae phytoplankton population and spurred a huge growth in zooplankton populations. The vast amount of primary production has created a distinguishable difference in DO levels between the epilimnion and hypolimnion characteristic of a eutrophic system.
